question.text: The 'internal contradiction' in the concept of market efficiency, discussed in the chapter, refers to which paradox?

answer.text: Markets become efficient only because profit-seeking participants BELIEVE they are inefficient and actively trade to exploit opportunities - if everyone gave up active search, efficiency would collapse.
Regulators impose efficiency by mandating identical information disclosure to all investors.
Markets are efficient in theory but completely random in practice, making both sides of the debate equivalent.
Efficiency only exists on holidays when no trading takes place.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Ch 3.5.3, markets do not become efficient on their own - they become efficient BECAUSE large numbers of profit-maximising participants believe they are inefficient and trade aggressively on information. This requires deep, liquid markets and is the internal (Grossman-Stiglitz-type) contradiction. The Trap: Option B confuses regulation with market mechanism. Option C is nihilistic nonsense. Option D is obviously wrong. Cross-Exam Context: XV (RA), XXI-B (PM) reference Grossman-Stiglitz (1980). XIX-C angle: this paradox is WHY sophisticated active AIF managers still extract alpha - particularly in thinner, less-covered pockets like Indian small-caps, private credit and VC. Manager's Pro-Tip: Use this paradox when defending your active management fee: your fund's very existence helps push prices toward efficiency - LPs are paying for that price-discovery function, especially in illiquid private markets.
